name: The Retail Unlock: Selling Private Markets to Main Street
deck: Alternative asset managers are distributing private equity, private credit, and infrastructure funds to individual investors, shifting illiquidity risk from pension funds to retail wealth channels.
core_bet: Large alternative managers (KKR, Blackstone, Invesco, Franklin Resources) have exhausted institutional LP capacity and are now selling private-market exposure through registered investment advisors and wealth channels. This widens the fee base while redistributing illiquidity risk and complexity onto retail-adjacent investors who lack institutional liquidity buffers.
mechanism: The institutional LP pool reached saturation by 2024-2025. Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and endowments could only deploy so much capital into private equity, infrastructure, and credit. Large managers responded by opening new channels: K-Series (KKR's retail offering), BREIT (Blackstone's retail real-estate product), Franklin's alternatives distribution through advisors, and Invesco's private-markets access through wealth platforms. This move from institutional to retail is not charitable—it shifts the burden.

Retail illiquidity risk far exceeds institutional buffers. An institutional LP gate capital and redemptions carefully. A retail investor in BREIT or a K-Series fund faces mark-to-market volatility, liquidity gates, and leverage risk that pension funds manage through dedicated staff and policy. The alternative manager collects fees regardless; the retail investor absorbs complexity.
why_now: Two drivers: first, record AUM growth meant managers needed new investor bases to continue scaling; second, wealth concentration made high-net-worth individuals and mass-affluent investors reachable through advisors. Fee pressure from passive indices made institutions less willing to pay 2-and-20; retail channels offered higher fees.
who_pays: Retail investors pay in higher fees, liquidity risk, and mark-to-market losses during downturns. They gain access to private markets but lose the institutional protections pension funds negotiate.
who_profits: Large alternative managers profit through higher AUM, wider fee bases, and ability to deploy more capital at lower marginal cost. The ability to distribute BREIT or K-Series to millions of retail accounts turbocharges AUM growth.
tension: If a recession or liquidity crisis occurs, retail investors may face illiquidity, mark-to-market losses, and potential redemption gates at the worst time. This concentrates systemic risk in retail channels that lack institutional buffers.
surprising_part: Retail demand for private markets proved stronger than expected. Investors actively sought private-market exposure despite illiquidity and complexity, suggesting either desperation for yield or genuine belief in private-market returns.
one_sentence: Private markets are being democratized downward in the capital stack, shifting illiquidity risk from institutions to retail.
societal_stake: Retail investors may be taking on structural risks they do not fully understand—liquidity, leverage, mark-to-market volatility—to capture returns that have historically been reserved for institutions with professional risk management.

evidence.fact: AUM reached $796B with fee-paying AUM of $638B in Q2 2026, record quarterly FRE and ANI per share
Record AUM of $1.346T in Q2 2026 with $68.3B inflows and explicit focus on wealth distribution and AI/infrastructure positioning
